question: What are the major findings on long COVID and the proposed mechanisms behind it?

statements.text: Viral persistence is implicated in long COVID, with SARS-CoV-2 spike antigen found in 60% of long COVID patients up to 12 months post-diagnosis versus 0% in recovered controls.

Immune dysregulation in long COVID includes exhausted T cells, elevated cytokines like IL-6 and TNF, activated innate immune cells, and alterations persisting at least 13 months after mild acute infection.

Approximately half of individuals with long COVID meet diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, with similar hemodynamic and cognitive abnormalities observed in both conditions.
Microclots and hyperactivated platelets are found in long COVID patients, contributing to thrombosis, endothelial dysfunction, and reduced vascular density persisting 18 months after infection.

Neurological mechanisms include neuroinflammation, microglial reactivity, myelin loss, reduced grey matter thickness, and brain hypometabolism correlated with cognitive symptoms in long COVID patients.
Low cortisol levels with inadequate compensatory ACTH response indicate hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction in long COVID patients more than one year after symptom onset.

Multiple autoantibodies are elevated in long COVID, targeting receptors including ACE2, muscarinic M2, and angiotensin receptors, though one major study did not find autoantibodies to be a major component.

Reactivated herpesviruses including EBV and HHV-6 are found in long COVID patients and are associated with fatigue, neurocognitive dysfunction, and mitochondrial fragmentation affecting energy metabolism.

Multi-organ damage occurs in long COVID, with 70% of patients showing damage to at least one organ and significantly increased risks of cardiovascular disease, adverse kidney outcomes, and type 2 diabetes.
Gut microbiota dysbiosis persists at least 14 months in long COVID, with low butyrate-producing bacteria strongly correlated with long COVID at 6 months and viral RNA persisting in stool samples.
POTS is found in 67% of one long COVID cohort, with dysautonomia commonly associated with G protein-coupled receptor autoantibodies and small fiber neuropathy.
Insufficient acute immune responses including low baseline IgG, low spike-specific memory B cells, and absent T cell responses predict long COVID development at 6-7 months post-infection.
